# Environment Variables

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/3.xdigging-deeper/env/

# Environment Variables

Declare your env keys once, in a typed class.

Then `env.appPort` is an `int`, your IDE suggests every key, and a missing key stops the app at startup.

## The typed env class

A new project already has `lib/config/env.dart`. Its keys are listed in the [Env reference](../reference/env.md#read-by-a-new-project). This example shows the kinds of getters you can write:

```dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'env.g.dart';

enum LogLevel { debug, info, error }

@DoxEnv()
abstract class AppEnv {
  static AppEnv load([EnvReader? reader]) {
    return _$AppEnv.load(reader);
  }

  String get appName;                       // APP_NAME, required
  String get appKey;                        // APP_KEY, required
  int get dbPort => 5432;                   // DB_PORT, default 5432
  bool get appDebug => false;               // APP_DEBUG, default false
  LogLevel get logLevel => LogLevel.info;   // LOG_LEVEL=debug
  Duration get cacheTtl => const Duration(minutes: 5); // CACHE_TTL=5m
  List<String> get corsOrigins => <String>[];          // CORS_ORIGINS=a.com,b.com

  @EnvKey('AWS_BUCKET')
  String? get s3Bucket;                     // optional, null when not set
}

/// The env of the app. Read and checked once, on first use.
final AppEnv env = AppEnv.load();
```

Run `dart run build_runner build` after each change to the class. It writes `env.g.dart`. Then use `env` anywhere:

```dart
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: 'postgres',
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(port: env.dbPort /* int */, ...),
  },
);
```

### The rules

- **Key**: the getter name in UPPER_SNAKE case. `appName` reads `APP_NAME`, `s3Bucket` reads `S3_BUCKET`. Use `@EnvKey('X')` for another name.
- **Default**: the getter body. It can be any expression, like `Platform.numberOfProcessors`. It runs only when the key is missing. A default can not read another env getter.
- **Optional**: a nullable getter with no body (`String? get s3Bucket;`). It is `null` when the key is missing.
- **Required**: any other getter with no body. A missing key stops the app.
- **Empty**: an empty value (or the text `null`) counts as missing.

### Types

| Type | Value in `.env` |
|------|-----------------|
| `String` | any text |
| `int`, `double`, `num` | `3000`, `0.5` |
| `bool` | `true`/`false`, `1`/`0`, `yes`/`no`, `on`/`off` (any case) |
| `Uri` | `https://dox.dev` |
| `Duration` | a number and a unit: `500ms`, `30s`, `5m`, `2h`, `1d`. A plain number is seconds: `300` is 5 minutes. |
| an enum | the name of a value, any case: `debug` |
| `List<String>` | comma separated: `a, b, c`. Empty items are dropped. |

Any other type is a build error.

### Fail fast

`AppEnv.load()` reads every key one time. Then it checks them all, and throws one `EnvException` that lists every missing or bad key:

```
EnvException: the env is not valid
  - APP_KEY is missing
  - DB_PORT must be an int, not "abc"
```

This happens once, when the app starts. After that, `env.dbPort` is a plain field read.

## Where values come from

Dox reads values from two places:

1. Real environment variables (set in the shell, Docker or systemd).
2. The `.env` file in the folder where you start the app. It is optional.

!!! info "The environment wins"
    A real environment variable wins over the `.env` file.
    So you can keep `.env` for development and use real variables in production.

### The `.env` file

```ini title=".env"
APP_NAME=dox
APP_KEY=change-me
DB_PORT=5432
```

- One `KEY=value` per line.
- Quotes around a value are removed. So `APP_NAME="My app"` gives `My app`. Use `"`, `'` or `` ` ``.
- A `=` inside the value is kept: `TOKEN=a=b` gives `a=b`.
- A line that starts with `#` is a comment.
- A `#` after a space starts a comment: `APP_PORT=3000 # dev` gives `3000`.
- A `#` with no space before it is kept: `DB_PASSWORD=abc#123` gives `abc#123`.
- A `#` inside quotes is kept: `DB_PASSWORD="abc # 123"` gives `abc # 123`.

## Commands

```bash
dox env:generate   # make lib/config/env.dart from .env.example
dox env:check      # load the env and print every missing or bad key
```

`dox env:generate` reads `.env.example`:

- digits become an `int` with that default: `APP_PORT=3000` gives `int get appPort => 3000;`
- `true`/`false` become a `bool` with that default
- an empty value becomes an optional `String?`
- any other value becomes a required `String`. The example value is never a default, so a secret in the example can not leak into the code.
- `#` comment lines above a key become its doc comment

It does not overwrite an existing `lib/config/env.dart`. Run `dox build_runner:build` after it.

`dox env:check` exits with code 1 when a key is missing or bad. Use it in CI or before a deploy.

## Tests

To pass your own values in a test, see [Testing](testing.md#test-the-env).

## Env.get: the low-level way

`Env.get()` reads one key by name. Use it for a key you only know at run time. For normal config, use the typed class.

```dart
Env.get<String>('APP_KEY');             // '' when missing
Env.get('APP_KEY', 'default_value');
Env.get<int>('APP_PORT', 3000);
Env.get<bool>('SOCKETIO_ENABLED', false); // true, 1, yes, on
Env.get<String?>('AWS_BUCKET');          // null when it is not set
```

A missing or empty key gives the default. With no default:

- `String` gives an empty string `''`. It is never the text `"null"`.
- `String?` and `dynamic` give `null`. With no type, like `Env.get('KEY')`, the type is `dynamic`, so you get `null`.
- `int`, `num`, `double` and `bool` throw an `ArgumentError` with the key name. A value that is not a number throws too.

`Env.get()` looks up and converts the value on every call. Do not call it on a hot path.

!!! warning "APP_KEY"
    When `APP_KEY` is missing, not 32 characters, or a public sample key, `Dox().startServer()` stops with an error.
    When `APP_ENV` is `development`, `local` or `test`, it only logs a warning. Make a key with `dox key:generate`.


---

# Isolate

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/3.xdigging-deeper/isolate/

# Isolate

This page explains how Dox runs your app on many isolates (threads), and what that means for your code.

## How it works

Dox starts many isolates. Each one runs its own [native server](native-server.md) on the same port. The operating system spreads the connections between them.

- Linux: each isolate has its own socket (`SO_REUSEPORT`).
- macOS: the isolates share one socket.
- Windows: only one isolate serves HTTP.

Each isolate has its own Rust acceptor on the port:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    OS["Port 3000<br>the OS spreads the connections"] --> A1["Rust acceptor"]
    OS --> A2["Rust acceptor"]
    OS --> A3["Rust acceptor"]
    A1 --> I1["Isolate 1, main<br>own memory cache"]
    A2 --> I2["Isolate 2<br>own memory cache"]
    A3 --> I3["Isolate N<br>own memory cache"]
    I2 -. "crash: started again after 1 second" .-> I2
    I1 -. "crash: the process exits" .-> S["Supervisor restarts the process<br>Docker, systemd"]
```

With the Postgres and MySQL drivers, all isolates share one database pool in Rust. See [How Dox works](../concepts/how-dox-works.md#where-the-database-pools-live).

## How many isolates

By default Dox starts one isolate per CPU core (`Platform.numberOfProcessors`).

To change it, set `totalIsolate` in `lib/config/app.dart`. A new app reads it from `APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  totalIsolate: env.appTotalIsolate ?? Platform.numberOfProcessors,
);
```

You can also set it in code, before `startServer()`. This wins over the config:

```dart title="bin/server.dart"
Dox().initialize(appConfig);
Dox().totalIsolate(2);
await Dox().startServer();
```

Use fewer isolates when:

- the machine also runs the database or other heavy work, or
- you use Socket.IO rooms without the Redis adapter. A room only reaches clients on the same isolate. Use `1`, or see [Socket.IO](../packages/socketio.md).

## Each isolate has its own memory

Isolates do not share memory:

- A static value or a singleton exists once **per isolate**. When you change it in one isolate, the others do not see it.
- The `memory` cache store is per isolate. See [Cache](cache.md).
- To share data between isolates or servers, use a database, Redis or files.

`Dox().isolateId` tells you which isolate runs the code. The first isolate is `1`.

## What each isolate does at start

Dox copies the `AppConfig`, the services and the routes you added before `startServer()` to each new isolate. Then every isolate:

1. runs `setup()` of each service (for example, it opens the database pool),
2. registers the routes of your routers,
3. reads the parameter types of each controller once,
4. starts its HTTP server.

Because the config and services are copied, they must not hold open sockets or database pools. Open these in `setup()`. See [Services](services.md).

## When an isolate crashes

- An error in a request is caught. Dox sends a `500` and keeps going.
- An async error outside a request (for example a future that nobody awaits) is caught and passed to the `report` method of the [exception handler](../the-basic/errors.md). The isolate keeps running.
- If a worker isolate still dies, Dox prints `[dox] isolate N exited, restarting` to stderr. It starts a new isolate after 1 second.
- If the first (main) isolate dies, the process exits with a non-zero code. Let a supervisor start it again, like Docker `restart:` or systemd `Restart=always`. See [Deployment](deployment.md#keep-it-running).


---

# Services

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/3.xdigging-deeper/services/

# Services

A service is a class with a `setup()` method. Dox runs it at start, in every isolate.

Use it to set up things like the database or auth.

## Why services

Dox runs your app on many [isolates](isolate.md), and they do not share memory.
Code that you run once in `bin/server.dart` only sets up the first isolate. The others have, for example, no database connection.
A service fixes this: each isolate runs `setup()` itself.

## Create a service

Implement `DoxService` and put your code in `setup()`. `setup()` can be `async`. Dox waits for it.

```dart title="lib/services/orm_service.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

class ORMService implements DoxService, DoxShutdown {
  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig);
  }

  /// Close the database connections when the server stops.
  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await SqlQueryBuilder.close();
  }
}
```

## Register it

You do not need to. Dox finds every class that implements `DoxService`.
Run `dart run build_runner build`. The service is then in `lib/container.g.dart`.
Each isolate makes its own instance from the container. Its constructor can ask for other classes of the container.
See [Dependency injection](../the-basic/dependency-injection.md#routers-and-services).

Services run in the order of their file path. To run one first, list it in `AppConfig`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  container: registerContainer,
  services: <DoxService>[ORMService()], // runs before the others
);
```

A listed service runs first. Then the others run. No service runs twice.

You can also add a service in code, before `startServer()`:

```dart title="bin/server.dart"
Dox().initialize(appConfig);
Dox().addService(MyService());
await Dox().startServer();
```

## Example: auth

```dart title="lib/services/auth_service.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class AuthService implements DoxService {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(AuthConfig(
      defaultGuard: 'web',
      guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
        'web': AuthGuard(
          driver: JwtAuthDriver(secret: SecretKey(env.appKey)),
          provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
        ),
      },
    ));
  }
}
```

See [Authentication](../security/authentication.md).

## When `setup()` runs

In each isolate, Dox runs `setup()` of each service, one after the other: the listed ones first, then the ones of the container.
Then it registers the routes and starts the server, so routes can use what a service set up.
See [What each isolate does at start](isolate.md#what-each-isolate-does-at-start).

`dox openapi:generate` also runs `setup()` of every service, because it needs the routes.

## Clean up on shutdown

On `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT` Dox stops the server gracefully (see [Deployment](deployment.md#graceful-shutdown)).
After the open requests are done, it runs `shutdown()` of each service that also implements `DoxShutdown`.
It runs in every isolate. Use it to close connections or flush data.

The `ORMService` of a new project already does this: its `shutdown()` calls `SqlQueryBuilder.close()`.
Dox closes the cache stores (eg. Redis) by itself, after the services.

```dart title="lib/services/redis_service.dart"
class RedisService implements DoxService, DoxShutdown {
  late RedisConnection redis;

  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    redis = await RedisConnection.open();
  }

  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await redis.close();
  }
}
```

An error in `shutdown()` goes to the `report` method of the [exception handler](../the-basic/errors.md). The other services still run.

## Rules for a service

- **Open connections in `setup()`, not in the constructor.** A service listed in `AppConfig` is copied to each isolate. An open socket or database pool can not be copied, so the isolate fails to start.
- **Keep `setup()` short.** It runs once per isolate. Data you load in it is kept once per isolate, so 8 isolates keep 8 copies.


---

# Dox CLI

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/3.xdigging-deeper/dox-cli/

# Dox CLI

The `dox` CLI creates projects and files, runs the dev server, builds for production and runs migrations.

Run `dox help` to see all commands. Run `dox help <command>` for one command.

## Installation

```bash
dart pub global activate dox ^3.0.0-alpha
```

!!! warning "Add the pub bin folder to your PATH"
    If your shell can not find `dox`, add this line to `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc`, and open a new terminal:

    ```bash
    export PATH="$PATH":"$HOME/.pub-cache/bin"
    ```

To remove the CLI:

```bash
dart pub global deactivate dox
```

## All commands

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `dox create <name> [--version <v>]` | create a new project |
| `dox serve` (or `dox s`) | start the dev server with build_runner watch |
| `dox build` | build the native (AOT) bundle into `build/bundle` |
| `dox build_runner:watch` / `dox build_runner:build` | run the code generator |
| `dox create:controller <name> [-r]` | create a controller |
| `dox create:middleware <name>` | create a middleware |
| `dox create:dto <name>` | create a DTO (typed, checked input) |
| `dox create:serializer <name>` | create a serializer |
| `dox create:model <name> [-m]` (or `make:model`) | create a model, and with `-m` its migration |
| `dox make:migration <name> [--sql]` (or `create:migration`) | create a Dart migration, or a `.sql` one with `--sql` |
| `dox migration:run` (or `dox migrate`) | run new migrations |
| `dox migration:rollback [--step=N]` | undo the last batch, or the last N migrations |
| `dox migration:reset` | undo all migrations |
| `dox migration:refresh` | undo all, then run all again |
| `dox migration:fresh` (or `migrate:fresh`) | drop all tables, then run all migrations |
| `dox migration:status` | show which migrations ran, and their batch |
| `dox make:factory <model>` | create a model factory in `db/factories`, see [Factories](../database/factories.md) |
| `dox make:seeder <name>` | create a seeder in `db/seeders`, see [Seeders](../database/seeders.md) |
| `dox db:seed [--class=<name>]` | run `DatabaseSeeder`, or another seeder |
| `dox key:generate` | make a new `APP_KEY` |
| `dox env:generate` | make `lib/config/env.dart` (the typed env class) from `.env.example`, see [Environment Variables](env.md) |
| `dox env:check` | check the env against `lib/config/env.dart`. Prints every missing or bad key (exit code 1) |
| `dox openapi:generate [dir]` | write `openapi.json` and `openapi.yaml` (default `storage/openapi`), see [OpenAPI](../packages/openapi.md#write-the-files-dox-openapigenerate) |
| `dox update` | update the CLI |
| `dox version` (or `dox -v`) | show the CLI version |
| `dox help [command]` | show help |

## Project

### Create a project

```bash
dox create new_blog
dox create new_blog --version v3.0.0-alpha.5
```

`dox create` copies the [dox-sample](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-sample) template from GitHub. Without `--version`, it uses the newest template release with the same major version as the CLI.

### Run the dev server

```bash
dox serve                         # or: dox s
dox s --ignore-build-runner       # do not run build_runner watch
```

`dox serve` runs `dart run bin/server.dart` and restarts it when a `.dart` file changes.
It also runs `build_runner watch`, so generated files stay up to date.

### Build for production

```bash
dox build
cd build/bundle
./bin/server
```

See [Deployment](deployment.md#build).

## Create files

```bash
dox create:controller Blog        # lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart
dox create:controller Blog -r     # resource controller
dox create:middleware Auth
dox create:dto CreateBlog         # lib/app/http/dtos/create_blog.dto.dart
dox create:serializer Blog
dox create:model Blog -m          # model and its create_blogs_table migration
dox make:migration create_blogs_table          # .dart file (default)
dox make:migration create_blogs_table --sql    # .sql file
```

- `-r` adds the methods `index`, `create`, `store`, `show`, `edit`, `update` and `destroy`.
- Word breaks are kept. `BlogPost` makes `blog_post.controller.dart` with the class `BlogPostController`.
- After `create:dto`, run `dox build_runner:build`. See [Validation](../the-basic/validation.md).
- The table of a model is its name in plural snake case: `BlogPost` makes `blog_posts`. The model gets `@DoxModel(table: 'blog_posts')`.

## Migrations

### Database settings

The migration commands read the database settings from the `.env` file and the real environment. A real environment variable wins.

```ini title=".env"
# postgres, mysql or sqlite
DB_CONNECTION=postgres
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
# for sqlite: the file path
DB_NAME=postgres
DB_USERNAME=admin
DB_PASSWORD=password
```

- `DB_CONNECTION` defaults to `postgres`. The default port is `5432` for postgres and `3306` for mysql.
- `DB_DATABASE` works too, in place of `DB_NAME`.
- Put comments on their own line. A `#` after a value becomes part of the value.

All keys are in the [Env reference](../reference/env.md#read-by-the-framework).

### Run and undo migrations

```bash
dox migration:run                # or: dox migrate
dox migration:status
dox migration:rollback           # undo the last batch
dox migration:rollback --step=2  # undo the last 2 migrations
dox migration:reset              # undo all migrations
dox migration:refresh            # undo all migrations, then run them again
dox migration:fresh              # drop all tables, then run all migrations
```

`migrate:rollback`, `migrate:reset`, `migrate:refresh`, `migrate:fresh` and `migrate:status` also work.
Add `--seed` to `migration:run`, `migration:refresh` or `migration:fresh` to run the seeders after it.

- A failed migration stops the run, and the CLI exits with code 1.
- On MySQL, statements like `CREATE`, `ALTER` and `DROP` save right away. So when a migration fails half way, these changes are not undone.

## Update the CLI

`dox update` installs the newest version with the same major version as your CLI, previews included.
To pick the version yourself, run the install command again.


---

# Deployment

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/3.xdigging-deeper/deployment/

# Deployment

This page shows how to build a Dox app for production and run it safely.

!!! danger "Never run production with `dart run`"
    `dart run` (and `dox serve`) uses the JIT compiler. It is made for
    development. It uses about 25x more memory at start (around 390 MB
    instead of 16 MB) and starts slower. Always build an AOT binary for
    production.

## Build

```bash
dox build
```

This makes a `build/bundle/` folder:

| File                        | What it is                                       |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `build/bundle/bin/server`   | the native binary. No Dart SDK needed to run it  |
| `build/bundle/lib/`         | native libraries from build hooks (eg. SQLite)   |
| `build/bundle/db/`          | your migrations                                  |
| `build/bundle/.env.example` | copy it to `build/bundle/.env`, or use env variables |

`dox build` runs `build_runner` (when your app uses it), then
`dart build cli --target bin/server.dart --output build`. It exits with code 1
when a step fails, so CI can stop.

!!! warning "Not `dart compile exe`"
    `dox_orm` depends on `sqlite3` v3. It bundles SQLite with a build hook.
    `dart compile exe` does not run build hooks, so it stops with an error.
    `dart build cli` is the same AOT compiler and runs the hooks.
    Keep `bin/` and `lib/` together: the binary loads the libraries from `../lib`.

Start it:

```bash
cd build/bundle
./bin/server
```

The binary reads `.env` and `db/` from the folder you start it in.
A real environment variable wins over the `.env` file.

A new Dox app runs the migrations in `bin/server.dart`, before the server starts.
So the database is up to date when the first request comes in.

## Docker

A new Dox app has this multi-stage `Dockerfile`. The final image is `FROM scratch`: only the Dart AOT runtime, the bundle, `db/` and an empty `/tmp`.

```dockerfile
FROM dart:stable AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY pubspec.* ./
RUN dart pub get
COPY . .
RUN dart pub get --offline
RUN dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
RUN dart build cli --target bin/server.dart --output build
RUN mkdir -p /out/app/storage /out/tmp \
  && chmod 1777 /out/tmp \
  && cp -r build/bundle/. /out/app/ \
  && cp -r db /out/app/db

FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /runtime/ /
COPY --from=build /out/ /
WORKDIR /app
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["/app/bin/server"]
```

The image has no `.env` file, so secrets stay out of it. Pass config as
environment variables:

```bash
docker build -t my-app .
docker run -p 3000:3000 -e APP_PORT=3000 -e APP_KEY=... -e DB_HOST=... my-app
```

Or use `env_file: .env` in `docker-compose.yml`.

## HTTPS: put a proxy in front

Do not serve HTTPS from Dart. TLS in Dart's `HttpServer` is slow (a known
Dart SDK issue). Dox has no `bindSecure`.

Run Dox on plain HTTP on a private port. Put [Caddy](https://caddyserver.com)
or nginx in front of it. The proxy does TLS, HTTP/2 and gzip.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C["Client"] -->|HTTPS| X["Caddy or nginx<br>TLS, HTTP/2, gzip, body size limit"]
    X -->|"plain HTTP on 127.0.0.1:3000"| D["Dox binary<br>bin/server, one isolate per core"]
    D -->|"one shared pool"| DB[("Database")]
    M["Migrations<br>bin/server.dart runs them once, before the server starts"] --> DB
```

Then tell Dox to trust the proxy, so `req.ip()` and `req.scheme()` show the
real client:

```dart
AppConfig(
  /// the proxy's IP, or a range like '10.0.0.0/8', or '172.16.0.0/12' for docker
  trustedProxies: <String>['127.0.0.1', '::1'],
);
```

- `req.ip()` reads `X-Forwarded-For`. Dox walks the list from the right and
  skips your proxies, so a fake value from the client is ignored.
- `req.scheme()` reads `X-Forwarded-Proto` (`http` or `https`).
  `req.isSecure()` is true for `https`.
- `trustedProxies` is empty by default. Then Dox ignores those headers,
  because any client can send them.
- `['*']` trusts any direct client. Only use it when the app port is not
  reachable from outside. With `*`, `req.ip()` is the right-most
  `X-Forwarded-For` hop, the one your proxy added. If you have two proxies
  in a row, list their IPs or ranges instead.

### Caddy

Caddy gets a certificate for you and sets `X-Forwarded-For` and
`X-Forwarded-Proto`. Websockets work with no extra config.

```
example.com {
  encode gzip
  reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:3000
}
```

### Nginx

```nginx
upstream dox {
  server 127.0.0.1:3000;
  keepalive 64;
}

map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
  default upgrade;
  ''      '';
}

server {
  listen 443 ssl http2;
  server_name example.com;

  ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem;
  ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem;

  # match maxMultipartSize in AppConfig
  client_max_body_size 100m;

  gzip on;
  gzip_types application/json text/plain text/css application/javascript;

  location / {
    proxy_pass http://dox;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;

    # websocket upgrade
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;

    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

    # stream uploads to Dox, do not buffer them in nginx first
    proxy_request_buffering off;
  }
}

server {
  listen 80;
  server_name example.com;
  return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
}
```

## Keep it running

When a worker isolate dies, Dox starts it again. When the main isolate dies,
the process exits with a non-zero code (see [Isolate](isolate.md#when-an-isolate-crashes)).
Let a supervisor restart it: `restart: unless-stopped` in Docker compose,
or `Restart=always` in systemd.

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/dox.service
[Service]
WorkingDirectory=/srv/app/build/bundle
ExecStart=/srv/app/build/bundle/bin/server
EnvironmentFile=/srv/app/build/bundle/.env
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

## Graceful shutdown

On `SIGTERM` (docker stop, Kubernetes, Cloud Run, Fly, systemd) or `SIGINT` (Ctrl+C), Dox stops gracefully, in every isolate:

1. It stops taking new connections at once.
2. Open requests can finish. Each keep-alive connection closes after its current answer.
3. After `shutdownTimeout` (default 8 seconds), it closes the connections that are still open.
4. It runs `shutdown()` of each service that implements `DoxShutdown` (see [Services](services.md#clean-up-on-shutdown)). The `ORMService` of a new project closes the database connections here.
5. It closes the cache stores of `Cache()`, eg. the Redis connections.
6. The process exits with code `0`.

A second `SIGINT` or `SIGTERM` stops the process at once.

Set the timeout in `lib/config/app.dart`:

```dart
AppConfig(
  shutdownTimeout: Duration(seconds: 20),
  ...
)
```

Keep it shorter than the time your platform waits before it kills the process:

| Platform | Waits | Change it with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `docker stop` | 10 seconds | `docker stop -t 30`, or `stop_grace_period` in compose |
| Kubernetes | 30 seconds | `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` |
| Cloud Run | 10 seconds | can not be changed |
| Fly.io | 5 seconds | `kill_timeout` in `fly.toml` |
| systemd | 90 seconds | `TimeoutStopSec` |

In code, `await Dox().stop()` does steps 1 to 4 and does not exit.

## Many processes or machines

One Dox process already uses every core. You only need more processes to
run on more machines, or to restart one process without downtime.
Run each one on its own port (or machine) and list them in the proxy:

```nginx
upstream dox {
  server 10.0.0.11:3000;
  server 10.0.0.12:3000;
  keepalive 64;
}
```

Socket.IO rooms then need a shared adapter (like Redis), because each
process has its own memory.


---

# Native server

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/3.xdigging-deeper/native-server/

# Native server

Dox runs on a native HTTP server from the package `dox_http_native`.

You do not need to set anything. Every app uses it, also an app with
WebSocket or Socket.IO routes.

- Rust ([hyper](https://hyper.rs)) owns the sockets and parses HTTP.
- All your code stays in Dart: routes, controllers, DTOs, middleware, ORM.
- It is much faster than the `dart:io` server. In a hello world test on one
  core it served about 5 times more requests. See [Performance](performance.md).

You do not need Rust. The package downloads a ready-built library for your
system when you build the app.

## How it works

1. Rust reads the requests from the sockets.
2. It sends the requests to Dart in batches (one message per batch).
3. Dart runs your handlers.
4. Dart sends all answers back to Rust in one call.

The native server has the same API as the `dart:io` `HttpServer`. So
`req.httpRequest`, `HttpResponse` and code written for `dart:io` keep working.

Each isolate runs its own server on the same port. See [Isolate](isolate.md).
The OS spreads connections, not requests. A keep-alive connection stays on
one isolate. So a few busy connections (eg. from one proxy or a load test
with few connections) can keep some isolates idle. Use more connections
than isolates.

## When the library does not load

Dox stops at start, before any isolate runs. The error says why and how to
fix it:

```
Unsupported operation: dox_http_native did not load: <reason>.
Fix: install Rust (cargo, see https://rustup.rs), then run the app again ...
```

`<reason>` is for example `native library ABI 4, expected 5`: the library on
disk is from another version of the package. See
[Troubleshooting](../reference/troubleshooting.md#the-native-http-library-did-not-load).

## WebSocket

Rust also does the WebSocket upgrade and the WebSocket protocol.

1. Rust marks a request that asks for an upgrade.
2. Dart runs the route, the middleware and the `Origin` check, like for any
   request. A normal answer (eg. `403`) refuses the upgrade.
3. When Dart accepts, Rust sends the `101` answer. From then on Rust
   answers pings, does the close handshake, checks that text is UTF-8 and
   checks the size of each message.
4. Dart gets whole messages, in the same batches as requests. It sends
   messages back the same way as answers.

- A message or frame over the size limit closes the socket with code `1009`.
  Dart never reads it. `NativeWebSocket.upgrade` takes `maxMessageSize`. Socket.IO uses
  `maxHttpBufferSize`.
- Compression (permessage-deflate) is never agreed. A small compressed
  message could grow very big in memory.
- On a graceful stop (SIGTERM), every open WebSocket gets close code `1001`.
- In your own code, use `NativeWebSocket.upgrade(request)` from
  `dox_http_native`. It gives a `dart:io` `WebSocket`.

## Threads

Each isolate has its own Rust network thread. `DOX_HTTP_THREAD=shared` puts
all isolates on one thread. It is off by default: on 2 cores the one thread
was the limit and req/s fell by a quarter. Leave it off unless you measure
a gain.

## Limits

- Max size of the request line plus headers: 16 KB. Bigger gets `431`.
- A bad request gets `400`.
- A multipart form over `maxMultipartSize`, or any other body over
  `maxBodySize`, gets `413` from Rust. When `Content-Length` is too big and
  the client sent `Expect: 100-continue`, the `413` comes before the body is
  sent. Else Rust reads and drops the body first, so the client sees the
  `413`. Dart checks the limits again.
- A client that sends no body bytes for 120 seconds (idle time) gets `408`.
  A slow but steady upload is fine.
- A small response is sent in one piece when it is closed. A streamed
  response (a file, a download, any `Stream`) over 64 KB goes out in
  parts: the client gets the first bytes early. At most 1 MB of it waits
  in memory. Dart reads more of the file only when the client has read
  what was sent. When the client leaves, Dart stops reading.
- A request body of 64 KB or more goes to Dart without a copy.
- `compress: true` works: Rust gzips the body on another thread, so the
  isolate does not wait. A streamed response is not compressed.

## Where the library comes from

The build hook of `dox_http_native` (`hook/build.dart`) picks the first one
that works:

1. A path you give in the root `pubspec.yaml` of your app:

    ```yaml
    hooks:
      user_defines:
        dox_http_native:
          lib_path: /path/to/libdox_http_native.so
    ```

2. A local build in `native/target/release` of the package (for work on
   the package itself).
3. The ready-built library from the GitHub release, checked with sha256.
   There are builds for macOS (arm64, x64), Linux (x64, arm64) and
   Windows (x64).
4. A build from source with `cargo`, when Rust is installed.

When none works, the app still builds, but it stops at start with the
error above. Install Rust and run it again, so step 4 works.

!!! note "Use `dart build cli`"
    `dart compile exe` does not run build hooks. Use `dox build` or
    `dart build cli`. See [Deployment](deployment.md).

## Work on the native code

`dox_http_native` lives in its own repo:
[dartondox/dox-http-native](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-http-native).
The Rust code is in its `native` folder.

```bash
cd dox-http-native/native
cargo build --release   # the hook uses this build from now on
cargo test
cd .. && dart test --concurrency=1
```

To use your local copy in the Dox repo, or to release the package, see
[Contribute](../community/contribute.md#native-packages).


---

# Performance

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/3.xdigging-deeper/performance/

# Performance

This page shows how fast Dox is, and how to keep your app fast in production.

The short version:

1. Build with `dox build` and run the AOT binary. Never `dart run` in production.
2. Put Caddy or nginx in front for HTTPS and gzip.
3. Keep the default isolates (one per CPU core).
4. Keep the body limits on. Uploads stream to disk.

## Benchmark

A "hello world" test. Each server answers `GET /` with the plain text
`Hello World`. Dox is a small real Dox app with one route.

Hello world only measures framework overhead. A real app spends most of its
time on the database, JSON and your own code, so the gaps are much smaller
there.

### 1 core

| Server                        | req/s   | p99 ms | CPU % | peak MB |
| ----------------------------- | ------: | -----: | ----: | ------: |
| Dox, native server            | 171,042 | 0.92   | 100   | 9       |
| Dox, `dart:io` server         | 33,154  | 5.48   | 101   | 39      |
| Bun 1.4.3                     | 181,162 | 1.13   | 101   | 14      |
| Node 24.22.0                  | 81,909  | 2.26   | 101   | 54      |
| Pure Rust hyper (the ceiling) | 254,349 | 0.47   | 100   | 5       |

On one core, Dox with the native server is about as fast as Bun (0.94x).
It is 5x faster than Dox on `dart:io`.

How it was run:

- Docker on an Apple M2 (8 CPUs in the Docker VM), `linux/arm64`.
- The server and wrk run in two containers, pinned to different CPUs:
  server on CPU 0, wrk on CPUs 2-7.
- wrk 4.2.0, 100 connections (the tables) and 256 connections.
  5 seconds warm-up, then 3 runs of 10 seconds. The tables show the median.
- CPU % and peak memory come from `docker stats`. 100% = one core.
- Dart 3.13.6, Rust 1.99.1. Dox is built with `dart build cli` (this is
  what `dox build` does). The build hook of `dox_http_native` builds the
  Rust library with cargo.
- The `dart:io` row is the same Dox app on a `dart:io` `HttpServer`, for
  comparison.

## App benchmark

A small real app, the same in each language: `GET /json` returns a map,
`GET /db` reads one row by id from Postgres, `GET /queries?n=20` reads 20
rows one after another. The table has 10,000 rows. Each server runs alone
on one or two pinned CPUs, Postgres 18 and wrk on other CPUs, 256
connections, 4 database connections per core, 3 runs of 10 seconds, median.
Versions: Dox 3.0.0-alpha.3 (native server, `dox_postgres_native`), Go 1.27
(`net/http` + pgx), Bun 1.4 (`Bun.serve` + `Bun.sql`), Node 24
(`node:http` + `pg`), `dart:io` (`HttpServer` + `package:postgres`).

  <span></span><span></span>
  <span class="dox-bench__head">req/s</span>

  <div class="dox-bench__row dox-bench__row--win">
    <span class="dox-bench__name"><strong>Dox</strong><span>2 isolates</span></span>
    <span class="dox-bench__track"><span class="dox-bench__bar" style="--w: 100%"></span></span>
    <span class="dox-bench__num">12,902<span class="dox-bench__vs">fastest</span></span>
  </div>
  <div class="dox-bench__row">
    <span class="dox-bench__name"><strong>Bun</strong><span>2 workers</span></span>
    <span class="dox-bench__track"><span class="dox-bench__bar" style="--w: 85.3%"></span></span>
    <span class="dox-bench__num">11,006<span class="dox-bench__vs">1.2× slower</span></span>
  </div>
  <div class="dox-bench__row">
    <span class="dox-bench__name"><strong>Node</strong><span>2 workers + pg</span></span>
    <span class="dox-bench__track"><span class="dox-bench__bar" style="--w: 45.5%"></span></span>
    <span class="dox-bench__num">5,870<span class="dox-bench__vs">2.2× slower</span></span>
  </div>
  <div class="dox-bench__row">
    <span class="dox-bench__name"><strong>Go</strong><span>net/http + pgx</span></span>
    <span class="dox-bench__track"><span class="dox-bench__bar" style="--w: 39.8%"></span></span>
    <span class="dox-bench__num">5,134<span class="dox-bench__vs">2.5× slower</span></span>
  </div>
</div>

<p class="dox-bench__foot"><span>Dox 3.0.0-alpha.3 · Bun 1.4 · Go 1.27 · Node 24 · Postgres 18 · 256 connections · wrk · median of 3 runs</span></p>

</div>

| Route            | Dox     | Bun     | Go      | Node    |
| ---------------- | ------: | ------: | ------: | ------: |
| /json req/s      | 251,427 | 385,553 | 175,009 | 156,389 |
| /db req/s        | 138,514 | 128,998 | 49,393  | 61,611  |
| /queries req/s   | 12,902  | 11,006  | 5,134   | 5,870   |
| /db p99 ms       | 3.62    | 5.61    | 8.53    | 8.06    |
| /db peak MB      | 51      | 57      | 22      | 297     |

Dox runs one isolate per core, Bun and Node one worker process per core.
On the database routes Dox is ahead of all of them on 2 cores, and its p99
is the lowest. On `/json` Bun is faster: its server is C++ and calls the
JavaScript handler on the same thread, while Dox hands each batch of
requests from the Rust thread to the Dart isolate.

Dox on `dart:io` with the Dart `postgres` driver is 4 to 10 times slower
than Dox with the native server and driver. Keep both on.

### Dart VM flags

We tried a bigger young generation (`DART_VM_OPTIONS=--new_gen_semi_max_size=64`
and `128`) for a better p99. Over 5 runs the change was inside the noise,
and memory did not move. So there is no flag to set. Dox never sets VM
flags for you. `DART_VM_OPTIONS` is read by the AOT binary from
`dox build`, so you can try your own.

## Database drivers

One find-by-id query, AOT build (`dart build cli`), database on the same machine (Apple M-series), one isolate:

| Database | One query at a time | Many queries in flight | App CPU time per query |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Postgres 14 (4 connections) | 60 µs | 12.5 µs each (64 in flight) | |
| MySQL 8.4 (10 connections) | 67 µs | 11 µs each (32 in flight) | 13.5 µs |
| MariaDB 11 (10 connections) | 63 µs | 9.7 µs each (32 in flight) | 12.4 µs |

- The CPU time counts the Dart thread and the Rust thread. For MySQL, it is about 75,000 queries per second on one core.
- Dart sends many queries to Rust in one call. Rust sends many results back in one message.
- One query alone spends most of its time on the trip to the database. Many requests at the same time, like in a web server, get the most out of the driver.

## Bodies, uploads and big responses

These are on by default. You only need to keep them:

- A body over `maxBodySize` or `maxMultipartSize` gets `413` before it is all read. Set the same limit in the proxy. See [Size limits](../the-basic/request.md#size-limits).
- An upload over 1 MB streams to a temp file, so it does not fill the memory. See [Request](../the-basic/request.md#requestfile).
- A `File` or `Stream` response is streamed, not loaded into memory. See [Files and big responses](../the-basic/response.md#files-and-big-responses).

## gzip

gzip in Dart is off by default.

```dart
AppConfig(compress: true);
```

- It saves bandwidth, but costs CPU on every response. The native server
  gzips on a Rust thread. Streamed responses are not compressed.
- A proxy (Caddy, nginx) does it better. Turn it on in Dart only when there
  is no proxy.
- With `compress: true`, text and JSON responses are sent chunked, without
  `Content-Length`.

## Logging

`LogMiddleware` prints one JSON line per request. Writing to stdout blocks
the isolate. So Dox collects log lines and writes them every 20 ms (or every
64 KB) in one write. If the process is killed hard, the last 20 ms of request logs can
be lost. Errors from `Logger` are still written right away.

Turn `LogMiddleware` off when a proxy already writes access logs. The new
project does this for you: `enabled` is `false` when `APP_ENV` is
`production`.

Leave `responseHandler` unset when you do not need it. With no handler, a
plain value (text, map, list) is sent without building a `DoxResponse`.

## What Dox does for you

- Routes are grouped by method. The regex of each route is built once, not
  on every request.
- The argument types of each controller are read once at start, not on
  every request.
- JSON and text responses are encoded once, straight to bytes, with
  `Content-Length` set.


---

# Testing

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/3.xdigging-deeper/testing/

# Testing

This page shows how to test a Dox app with the `test` package: HTTP routes, cache, storage, env and the database.

## Setup

Add the test package as a dev dependency:

```bash
dart pub add dev:test
```

Put your tests in the `test/` folder. Run them with:

```bash
dart test
```

## Test HTTP routes

`DoxTestClient` from `package:dox_core/testing.dart` starts your app inside the test and sends requests to it.

```dart title="test/http_test.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('GET /api/ping', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.get('/api/ping');
    res.expectStatus(200).expectBody('pong');
  });

  test('POST /api/posts', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.post(
      '/api/posts',
      body: <String, dynamic>{'title': 'Hello', 'body': 'My first post.'},
    );
    res.expectStatus(201).expectJson(containsPair('title', 'Hello'));
  });
}
```

- `DoxTestClient.start(appConfig)` runs your services (like the ORM service) and adds your routes, the same as a real start.
- It listens on `127.0.0.1` and a free port that the OS picks. So it does not clash with `dox serve`, and many test files can run at the same time.
- It runs on one isolate. `serverPort` and `totalIsolate` of the config are not used.
- `client.close()` stops the server and runs the `DoxShutdown` services (for example, it closes the database).
- With one isolate, you can also add a route inside a test with `Route.get(...)`. It works right away.

### Send requests

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `get(path)` | `GET`. The path can have a query: `'/api/users?page=2'`. |
| `post(path, body: ...)` | `POST`. Also `put`, `patch` and `delete`. |
| `send('OPTIONS', path)` | any other method |
| `headers: {...}` | extra headers for one request |
| `withHeaders({...})` | a copy of the client that sends these headers on every request |
| `withToken(token)` | a copy of the client that sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>` |

A `Map` or `List` body is sent as JSON. A `String` or `List<int>` body is sent as it is.
Redirects are not followed, so you can check a `302` and its `Location` header.

### Check the response

| Member | What it gives |
| --- | --- |
| `res.status` | the status code, like `200` |
| `res.body` | the body as text |
| `res.json` | the body read as JSON |
| `res.header('content-type')` | one header (any case) |
| `res.headers` | all headers, with lower case names |

The `expect` methods fail the test when the response is not right. They return the response, so you can chain them:

```dart
res
    .expectStatus(422)
    .expectHeader('content-type', contains('application/json'))
    .expectJson(<String, dynamic>{'title': 'The title is required'});
```

| Method | Fails when |
| --- | --- |
| `expectStatus(200)` | the status is another one. The message shows the body. |
| `expectJson(value or matcher)` | the JSON body does not match. Use a `Map`, or a matcher like `containsPair('id', 1)`. |
| `expectBody(value or matcher)` | the text body does not match |
| `expectHeader(name, value or matcher)` | the header does not match. Use `isNull` for "not there". |

### Log in as a user

Make a token, then send it with `withToken`:

```dart
TestResponse login = await client.post(
  '/api/auth/login',
  body: <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com', 'password': 'secret123'},
);
DoxTestClient ann = client.withToken(login.json['token'] as String);
(await ann.get('/api/auth/me')).expectStatus(200);
```

## Test the cache

`Dox().cache` is the `CacheManager` that `Cache()` uses. Replace it with a memory store, so tests do not write files or need Redis:

```dart
setUp(() {
  Dox().cache = CacheManager(CacheConfig(
    defaultStore: 'memory',
    stores: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
      'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory'},
    },
  ));
});

test('caches the posts', () async {
  await Cache().put('posts', <String>['a', 'b']);
  expect(await Cache().get('posts'), <dynamic>['a', 'b']);
});
```

A new `CacheManager` in `setUp` gives each test an empty cache. See [Cache](cache.md).

## Test file storage

`Dox().storage.fake(name)` swaps one disk with an empty memory disk. `restore(name)` puts the real disk back.

```dart
setUpAll(() {
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);
});

test('saves the report', () async {
  Disk fake = Dox().storage.fake('s3');

  String path = await Storage()
      .disk('s3')
      .put('reports', <int>[1, 2, 3], extension: 'pdf'); // '/reports/<uuid>.pdf'

  expect(await fake.exists(path.substring(1)), isTrue);
  Dox().storage.restore('s3');
});
```

- Call `Dox().initialize()` first. The storage disks are made from `appConfig`.
- `Storage()` paths start with `/`. A `Disk` key does not, so remove the first `/` when you ask the `Disk` directly.

See [File Storage](file-storage.md).

## Test the env

Pass your own values to `AppEnv.load()`. Then nothing is read from the shell or the `.env` file:

```dart
AppEnv env = AppEnv.load(
  EnvReader(
    environment: <String, String>{'APP_KEY': 'test'},
    dotEnv: <String, String>{'DB_PORT': '5433'},
  ),
);
expect(env.dbPort, 5433);
```

A missing or bad key throws an `EnvException`. So you can also test that your app stops on a bad env. See [Environment Variables](env.md).

## Test the database

A test that uses models needs a real database. Run the migrations once in `setUpAll`.
Then empty the tables before each test with `refreshDatabase()` from `package:dox_orm/testing.dart`:

```dart title="test/user_test.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    await Migrator(
      migrations: migrations,
      config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
    ).migrate();
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig); // runs the ORM service
  });

  // every test starts with empty tables
  setUp(refreshDatabase);

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('register makes a user', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.post(
      '/api/auth/register',
      body: <String, dynamic>{
        'name': 'Ann',
        'email': 'ann@example.com',
        'password': 'secret123',
      },
    );
    res.expectStatus(201);
  });
}
```

- `refreshDatabase()` empties every table and starts the ids at 1 again. The tables stay. It keeps the rows of the migrations table (`dox_db_migration`).
- It works on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. Foreign keys are not checked while it empties the tables.
- `refreshDatabase(keep: <String>['dox_db_migration', 'countries'])` keeps the rows of more tables.
- Use a separate test database. Set its name in the env of the test run, for example `DB_NAME=app_test dart test`. Never run it on a database with real data.
- A test without the server can start the ORM with `SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig)`.

See [Testing with a database](../guides/testing-with-database.md) for a full example with SQLite.

!!! tip "Run test files one by one"
    `dart test` runs test files at the same time. When two files use the same tables, run them one by one: `dart test --concurrency=1`.


---

# Health check

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/3.xdigging-deeper/health-check/

# Health check

A health route tells a load balancer, Docker or Kubernetes if the app can serve requests.

## Add the route

```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
Route.health('/health');
```

`GET /health` answers `200` with:

```json
{"status": "ok"}
```

## Check the database and the cache

Give named checks. Each check is a function:

```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

Route.health(
  '/health',
  checks: <String, HealthCheckFunction>{
    'database': () => QueryBuilder.query('select 1'),
    'cache': HealthCheck.cache(),
  },
);
```

When all checks pass, the answer is `200`:

```json
{"status": "ok", "checks": {"database": "ok", "cache": "ok"}}
```

When one check fails, the answer is `503 Service Unavailable`:

```json
{"status": "fail", "checks": {"database": "fail", "cache": "ok"}}
```

A check fails when it:

- throws an error,
- returns `false`,
- or takes longer than `timeout` (default 5 seconds).

The checks run at the same time.

- `HealthCheck.cache()` writes a key to the default cache store and reads it back. `HealthCheck.cache('redis')` checks the store with that name.
- Any other check is your own function, like a call to another API.

## Error details

The error of a failed check is passed to `exceptionHandler.report()`, so you see it in your logs.

The answer has the error text (in `errors`) only when `APP_ENV` is `development` or `local`.
In other envs the text is left out, because it can show hosts or user names.

## Change the timeout

```dart
Route.health(
  '/health',
  timeout: Duration(seconds: 2),
  checks: <String, HealthCheckFunction>{
    'database': () => QueryBuilder.query('select 1'),
  },
);
```

!!! tip
    A route in a router gets the middleware of that router and the global middleware.
    Put `Route.health` in a router with no auth middleware, or the health check gets `401`.

## See also

- [Docker](../guides/docker.md) for a health check in the image
- [Deployment](deployment.md)


---

# Database

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/3.xdatabase/

# Database

Connect Dox to Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB or SQLite with the `dox_orm` package.

- [Query builder](query-builder.md): build SQL with methods.
- [Models](model/index.md): one class per table.
- [Transactions](transactions.md): many queries that succeed or fail together.
- [Migration](migration.md) and [Schema](schema.md): create and change tables.

This is how a query travels from your code to the database:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    M["Model or QueryBuilder"] --> S["SQL text<br>quoted names, @values"]
    S --> D{"Driver"}
    D --> N["Native Rust pool<br>dox_postgres_native, dox_mysql_native"]
    D --> T["sqlite3"]
    N --> DB[("Database")]
    T --> DB
```

## Install

The query builder and the models are in the `dox_orm` package.

```bash
dart pub add dox_orm
```

```dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
```

## Supported databases

| Database | `Driver` | Driver | Pool | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Postgres | `Driver.postgres` | [`dox_postgres_native`](postgres-native.md) | Yes | Production |
| MySQL 8+ and MariaDB | `Driver.mysql` | [`dox_mysql_native`](mysql-native.md) | Yes | Production |
| SQLite | `Driver.sqlite` | `sqlite3` | No, one connection per isolate | Development, tests, small apps |

!!! info "Native drivers"
    Postgres and MySQL use a native (Rust) driver. There is no other driver.
    When the native library can not load, the app stops with an error.
    See the [Postgres](postgres-native.md#when-the-library-does-not-load) and
    [MySQL](mysql-native.md#when-the-library-does-not-load) pages.

## Config

Put the connections in `lib/config/database.dart`.
`connection` is the name of the default connection.

```dart title="lib/config/database.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: env.dbConnection,
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.postgres,
      host: 'localhost',
      port: 5432,
      user: 'postgres',
      password: 'postgres',
      database: 'postgres',
      extra: <String, dynamic>{'maxConnectionCount': 10},
      debug: false,
    ),
    'mysql': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.mysql, // also for MariaDB
      host: 'localhost',
      port: 3306,
      user: 'root',
      password: 'password',
      database: 'dox',
      extra: <String, dynamic>{'maxConnectionCount': 10},
      debug: false,
    ),
    'sqlite': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.sqlite,
      database: 'storage/app.db', // file path, or ':memory:'
      debug: false,
    ),
  },
);
```

- `debug: true` prints each SQL query and its values.
- `user`, `password`, `host` and `port` are not used by SQLite.

Start the ORM in a service. Each isolate runs the service.
Isolates with the same settings share one pool, so `maxConnectionCount` is for the whole process.

```dart title="lib/services/orm_service.dart"
class ORMService implements DoxService, DoxShutdown {
  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig);
  }

  /// Close the database connections when the server stops.
  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await SqlQueryBuilder.close();
  }
}
```

### `.env`

The app config and the [migration](migration.md) commands read these values.

```py title=".env"
DB_CONNECTION=postgres # postgres, mysql or sqlite
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432           # 3306 for mysql
DB_NAME=dox            # for sqlite: the file path, like storage/app.db
DB_USERNAME=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=postgres
```

### `DATABASE_URL`

Many hosts (Fly, Render, Heroku and others) give you one database url.
Dox reads it from the `DATABASE_URL` environment variable.

The rule: **when `DATABASE_URL` is set, it wins.**
It replaces the config of the default connection (`DatabaseConfig.connection`).
That config still gives `debug`, `printer` and `extra`.
Other named connections do not change.

```bash
DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:s%40cret@db.example.com:5432/blog?sslmode=require
```

| Form | Database |
|---|---|
| `postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db` or `postgresql://...` | Postgres |
| `mysql://user:pass@host:3306/db` or `mariadb://...` | MySQL, MariaDB |
| `sqlite:///abs/path.db`, `sqlite://db/dox.sqlite`, `sqlite::memory:`, `file:db/dox.sqlite` | SQLite |

- The user, password and database name are url-decoded. Write `@` in a password as `%40`.
- No port: `5432` for Postgres, `3306` for MySQL.
- For Postgres, `sslmode` works like libpq (`disable`, `prefer`, `require`, `verify-ca`, `verify-full`). `require` does not check the certificate. Use `verify-full` when your host supports it. See [Postgres TLS](postgres-native.md#tls).
- For MySQL, `ssl=true` (or `sslmode=require`) turns TLS on, and it checks the certificate. Add `verifyCertificate=false` to skip the check, only for a self-signed certificate in development.
- `host=/path` (or `socket=/path`) connects to a Unix socket, like `host=/cloudsql/project:region:instance`. See [Unix socket](#unix-socket).
- Any other option goes to `extra`, like `?maxConnectionCount=20`. A number becomes an `int`, `true` and `false` a `bool`.

The ORM reads `DATABASE_URL` from the real environment, not from `.env`.
To use a url from `.env`, or any other url, give it yourself:

```dart
DatabaseConfig(
  connection: 'postgres',
  connections: {...},
  url: Env.get<String?>('DATABASE_URL'),
);
```

An empty `url` (`url: ''`) turns `DATABASE_URL` off.
To make one `ConnectionConfig` from a url, use `ConnectionConfig.fromUrl(url)`.
[Migrations](migration.md#database-settings) read `DATABASE_URL` too, also from `.env`.

### Unix socket

A host that starts with `/` is a Unix socket.
Google Cloud SQL on Cloud Run uses `/cloudsql/PROJECT:REGION:INSTANCE`.

```bash
DB_HOST=/cloudsql/my-project:europe-west1:blog
# or
DATABASE_URL=postgres://blog:secret@/blog?host=/cloudsql/my-project:europe-west1:blog
```

**Postgres**: the host is the socket folder, like in libpq.
The driver uses the socket file `<folder>/.s.PGSQL.<port>`.
A host that already ends with `/.s.PGSQL.5432` works too.

**MySQL and MariaDB**: the host is the socket file itself. The port is not used.
On Cloud SQL, the socket file is `/cloudsql/PROJECT:REGION:INSTANCE`.
A local server often uses `/var/run/mysqld/mysqld.sock` or `/tmp/mysql.sock`.

```bash
DB_CONNECTION=mysql
DB_HOST=/var/run/mysqld/mysqld.sock
# or
DATABASE_URL=mysql://app:secret@/app?socket=/var/run/mysqld/mysqld.sock
```

`?socket=` and `?host=` do the same thing.

### `extra` options

`extra` is a map in `ConnectionConfig` for driver options.

| Key | Database | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `maxConnectionCount` | Postgres, MySQL | `10` | Most connections in the pool. |
| `threads` | Postgres, MySQL | `1` | Rust threads of the native driver. |
| `maxConnectionAge` | MySQL | 12 hours | A connection older than this is opened again. |
| `preparedStatementCacheSize` | MySQL, SQLite | `100` | Prepared statements kept per connection. |
| `sslMode` | Postgres | `disable` | TLS mode: `disable`, `prefer`, `require` or `verify-full`. |
| `sslRootCert` | Postgres | none | Path of a PEM file with the CA certificates to trust for `verify-full`. |
| `verifyCertificate` | MySQL | `true` | `false` skips the TLS certificate check. Only for development. |
| `timeZone` | Postgres | `UTC` | Time zone of the session. |
| `applicationName` | Postgres | none | Name of the app in `pg_stat_activity`. |
| `busyTimeout` | SQLite | `5000` | Milliseconds a query waits for a lock. |

### Table and column names are quoted

Table and column names you pass to `select`, `where`, `join`, `groupBy`, `orderBy`,
`insert` and `update` are quoted.
Postgres and SQLite use `"name"`. MySQL uses `` `name` ``.
So names like `order` or `key` work.

- `table.column`, `table.*`, `*` and `column as alias` are quoted in the right way.
- Anything else (for example `count(*) as total`) throws an `ArgumentError`.
  So user input can not add SQL.
- For expressions, use the raw methods (`selectRaw`, `whereRaw`, `orderByRaw`, `groupByRaw`, `joinRaw`).
- On Postgres, a quoted name is case sensitive. `userId` is not the same column as `userid`.

### Raw queries

`QueryBuilder.query()` runs SQL on the default connection.
Use `@name` for values. The values are sent as bound parameters.

```dart
List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.query(
  'select * from blog where id = @id',
  substitutionValues: <String, dynamic>{'id': 1},
);
```

Pass `connection` to run it on another connection.

```dart
await QueryBuilder.query('select 1', connection: 'mysql');
```

### Other connections

Use `withConnection()` with a connection name from the config.

```dart
List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('blog')
    .withConnection('mysql')
    .get();
```

A model keeps its connection. `save()` and `delete()` use it.
Models that a query returns use the connection of the query.

```dart
Blog blog = Blog()..withConnection('mysql');
blog.title = 'Hello';
await blog.save(); // saved on 'mysql'
```

## MySQL and MariaDB

- The driver is [`dox_mysql_native`](mysql-native.md). Its page lists how values are converted.
- `CREATE`, `ALTER` and `DROP` are saved right away. A transaction can not undo them.

## SQLite

SQLite is good for development, tests and small apps.
For a busy production app, use Postgres or MySQL.

!!! info "How it runs"
    The `sqlite3` package calls SQLite directly (FFI). A query blocks the isolate while it runs.
    Each isolate has one connection.
    The file uses WAL mode, so readers do not wait for the writer.
    `busyTimeout` makes a query wait for a lock from another isolate, instead of failing.
    Foreign keys are on.
    Before each `SELECT`, the driver checks `PRAGMA schema_version` to see if a table changed.

!!! info "Types"
    SQLite has no bool, JSON or date type. Dox converts them for you:

    - `boolean()` is saved as `0`/`1` and read back as `bool`.
    - `json()` is saved as text and read back as `Map` or `List`.
    - Dates are saved as ISO text in UTC and read back as `DateTime`.

    The driver uses the column type in `CREATE TABLE`.
    It finds the table by the table names in the query.
    So it works on tables made by `Schema`, or by SQL with the same type names
    (`BOOLEAN`, `JSON`, `TIMESTAMP`, `DATE`, `DATETIME`).
    A column with an alias (`active as is_active`) is not converted.

!!! warning "Limits"
    - Schema limits (`change()`, `dropColumn`, `NOT NULL` columns) are in [SQLite notes](schema.md#sqlite-notes).
    - `dropColumn` does not work on a primary key column.
    - `insertMultiple` with rows that have different keys inserts the rows one by one,
      because SQLite has no `DEFAULT` in `VALUES`.
    - SQLite before 3.39 has no `RIGHT JOIN`.

!!! info "Native library"
    The `sqlite3` package (v3) bundles SQLite with a build hook.
    You do not install a system library.
    For the AOT binary, use `dox build`. It puts the library in `build/bundle/lib/`,
    next to `build/bundle/bin/server`. Keep the two folders together.
    `dart compile exe` does not work with build hooks.
    See [Deployment](../digging-deeper/deployment.md).


---

# Query Builder

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/3.xdatabase/query-builder/

# Query Builder

The query builder makes SQL from chained methods and runs it with bound values on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite.

Set up the database first. See [Database](index.md).

## Start a query

There are two ways to start a query.

```dart
// with a model: the result is a list of Actor models
List<Actor> actors = await Actor().where('age', '>=', 23).get();

// with a table name: the result is a list of maps, one map per row
List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('actor')
    .where('age', '>=', 23)
    .get();
```

The examples on this page use an `Actor` model on the table `actor`.
The SQL in the examples is for Postgres. MySQL quotes names with `` ` `` instead of `"`.

!!! tip "Start each query with a new object"
    A query object keeps its `where`, `orderBy` and other parts.
    Use `Actor()` (or `QueryBuilder.table(...)`) again for each new query.

## Read rows

### `get`

Runs the query and returns all rows that match.

```dart
List<Actor> actors = await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').get();
// SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "name" = @name_p0
```

### `all`

Returns all rows of the table.
`all()` ignores `where`, `join`, `orderBy` and `limit`. Use `get()` for those.

```dart
List<Actor> actors = await Actor().all();
// SELECT * FROM "actor"
```

### `find`

Returns one row, or `null` when there is no match.

```dart
// by primary key
Actor? actor = await Actor().find(1);
// SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "id" = @id_p0 LIMIT 1

// by another column
Actor? byName = await Actor().find('name', 'John Wick');
// SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "name" = @name_p0 LIMIT 1
```

### `getFirst`

Returns the first row of the query, or `null`.

```dart
Actor? actor = await Actor().where('age', '>', 60).orderBy('age').getFirst();
// SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "age" > @age_p0 ORDER BY "age" LIMIT 1
```

### `count`

Returns the number of rows as an `int`.

```dart
int total = await Actor().count();
int adults = await Actor().where('age', '>=', 18).count();
// SELECT count(*) as total FROM "actor" WHERE "age" >= @age_p0
```

- `count()` ignores `limit`, `offset` and `orderBy`.
- With `groupBy`, `count()` returns the number of groups.

### `paginate`

Returns one page of rows and the page info.
It runs a `count()` query and a `get()` query.

```dart
Pagination<Actor> page = await Actor()
    .where('age', '>=', 18)
    .paginate(currentPage: 2, perPage: 10);

List<Actor> actors = page.data;
print(page.total);    // rows that match
print(page.lastPage); // number of pages
```

`page.toJson()` gives `total`, `per_page`, `last_page`, `current_page` and `data`.
So you can return a `Pagination` from a controller.

## Where

### `where`

```dart
// equal
await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').get();
// WHERE "name" = @name_p0

// other operator
await Actor().where('age', '>=', 23).get();
await Actor().where('name', '!=', 'John Wick').get();
await Actor().where('name', 'like', 'John%').get();

// null
await Actor().where('deleted_at', null).get();
// WHERE "deleted_at" IS NULL
```

Many `where` calls are joined with `AND`.

!!! info
    The operator must be one of `=`, `!=`, `<>`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `like`,
    `not like` or `ilike` (any case). Any other value throws an `ArgumentError`.
    The column must be a plain name. Use `whereRaw` for expressions.

### `orWhere`

```dart
await Actor().where('name', 'John Doe').orWhere('name', 'John Wick').get();
// WHERE "name" = @name_p0 OR "name" = @name_p1

await Actor().where('age', '<', 18).orWhere('age', '>', 60).get();
```

### `whereIn` and `whereNotIn`

```dart
await Actor().whereIn('id', <int>[1, 2]).get();
// WHERE "id" IN (@id_p0,@id_p1)

await Actor().whereNotIn('id', <int>[1, 2]).get();
await Actor().where('age', 60).orWhereIn('id', <int>[1, 2]).get();
await Actor().where('age', 60).orWhereNotIn('id', <int>[1, 2]).get();
```

- On Postgres, a list of only `int` or only `String` values is sent as one array
  parameter: `"id" = ANY(@id_p0)` (`<> ALL` for `whereNotIn`).
- An empty list matches no rows for `whereIn`, and all rows for `whereNotIn`.

### `whereNull` and `whereNotNull`

```dart
await Actor().whereNull('deleted_at').get();
await Actor().whereNotNull('deleted_at').get();
await Actor().where('age', 60).orWhereNull('deleted_at').get();
await Actor().where('age', 60).orWhereNotNull('deleted_at').get();
```

### `whereRaw` and `orWhereRaw`

Write the condition yourself. Put values in a map, and use `@key` in the SQL.
The column names are not quoted.

```dart
await Actor().whereRaw('name = @name', <String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Wick'}).get();

await Actor()
    .where('age', 60)
    .orWhereRaw('lower(name) = @name', <String, dynamic>{'name': 'john wick'})
    .get();
```

!!! warning
    Never put user input into the SQL text. Always send it in the map.

## Select

`select` sets the columns. Each call replaces the columns of the call before.

```dart
// a list
await Actor().select(<String>['id', 'name']).get();
// SELECT "id","name" FROM "actor"

// comma separated
await Actor().select('id, name, age').get();

// with an alias
await Actor().select('name as actor_name').get();

// raw: nothing is quoted
await Actor().selectRaw('DISTINCT name').get();
await QueryBuilder.table('actor').selectRaw('count(*) as total, name').groupBy('name').get();
```

Each part must be a plain name: `name`, `table.name`, `table.*`, `*` or `name as alias`.
Anything else, like `count(*)`, throws an `ArgumentError`. Use `selectRaw` for it.

!!! info
    A model loaded with `select()` only has the selected fields.
    `save()` on it only updates the fields it has.

## Order, limit and group

### `orderBy`

```dart
await Actor().orderBy('name').get();
await Actor().orderBy('name', 'desc').get();
await Actor().orderBy('name', 'asc').orderBy('id', 'desc').get();
// ORDER BY "name" asc,"id" desc
```

- The direction must be `asc` or `desc`. Any other value throws an `ArgumentError`.
- The column must be a plain name. Anything else throws an `ArgumentError`.
- For an expression, use `orderByRaw('count(*) desc')`. Nothing is quoted there,
  so never put user input in it.

### `limit`, `take` and `offset`

`limit` and `take` do the same thing.

```dart
await Actor().limit(10).get();
await Actor().take(10).get();
await Actor().limit(10).offset(20).get();
// LIMIT @dox_limit OFFSET @dox_offset
```

The numbers are sent as bound parameters.

### `groupBy`

Takes one column, or a list of columns.

```dart
List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('actor')
    .selectRaw('count(*) as total, age')
    .groupBy('age')
    .get();
```

For an expression, use `groupByRaw('date(created_at)')`. Nothing is quoted there.

!!! info
    Use `QueryBuilder.table()` for `groupBy`. A group row is a map, not a model.
    On a model, `get()` gives models (`List<Actor>`), so a `groupBy` there throws a `StateError`.
    `count()` with `groupBy` works on a model too.

## Join

```dart
await Actor().join('actor_info', 'actor_info.actor_id', 'actor.id').get();
// JOIN "actor_info" on "actor_info"."actor_id" = "actor"."id"

await Actor().leftJoin('actor_info', 'actor_info.actor_id', 'actor.id').get();
await Actor().rightJoin('actor_info', 'actor_info.actor_id', 'actor.id').get();

// with an operator
await Actor().join('actor_info', 'actor_info.actor_id', '=', 'actor.id').get();
```

For other join conditions, use the raw methods.
Nothing is quoted. Values go in the map, like in `whereRaw`.

```dart
await Actor().joinRaw('actor_info on actor_info.actor_id = actor.id').get();
await Actor().leftJoinRaw('actor_info on actor_info.actor_id = actor.id').get();
await Actor().rightJoinRaw(
  'actor_info on actor_info.actor_id = actor.id and actor_info.type = @type',
  <String, dynamic>{'type': 'main'},
).get();
```

!!! note
    SQLite before 3.39 has no `RIGHT JOIN`.

## Insert

### `create` and `insert`

`create` and `insert` do the same thing.
They insert one row, then read it back and return it.

```dart
Actor actor = await Actor().create(<String, dynamic>{
  'name': 'John Wick',
  'age': 60,
});
print(actor.id);
```

- On a model, the result is the model. On `QueryBuilder.table(...)`, the result is a map.
- It works with any primary key type, for example a uuid string.
- On a model with [events](model/events.md), `create` calls `save()`, so the hooks run.

### `insertMultiple`

Inserts many rows in one query.
It does not return models.
On Postgres it returns the new ids, like `[{id: 4}, {id: 5}]`.
On MySQL it returns only one id.

```dart
await Actor().insertMultiple(<Map<String, dynamic>>[
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Wick', 'age': 60},
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Doe', 'age': 25},
]);
```

The columns are the keys from all rows.
When a row does not have a key, that column gets its default value.

## Update

Updates all rows that match the `where` part.

```dart
await Actor()
    .where('id', 3)
    .where('status', 'active')
    .update(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'Updated AJ', 'age': 120});
// UPDATE "actor" SET "name" = @name_p2,"age" = @age_p3
//   WHERE "id" = @id_p0 AND "status" = @status_p1
```

!!! warning
    `update` without `where` changes every row of the table.
    A query `update` does not set `updated_at` and fires no [model events](model/events.md).
    To do that, load the model, change it and call `save()`.

## Delete

### `delete`

Deletes all rows that match the `where` part.

```dart
await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').delete();
// DELETE FROM "actor" WHERE "name" = @name_p0
```

On a model with `softDelete: true`, `delete` sets `deleted_at` and keeps the row.

### `forceDelete`

On a model with `softDelete: true`, `forceDelete` really deletes the rows.
It also deletes rows that are already soft deleted, so you do not need `withTrash()`.

```dart
await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').forceDelete();
```

### `withTrash`

A model with `softDelete: true` hides soft deleted rows.
`withTrash()` shows them too.
On a model without soft deletes it does nothing.

```dart
List<Actor> actors = await Actor().withTrash().where('name', 'John Wick').get();
```

### `truncate`

Deletes all rows of the table and resets the id counter.

```dart
await Actor().truncate();
await Actor().truncate(resetId: false); // keep the id counter on Postgres and SQLite
```

On Postgres it runs `TRUNCATE TABLE ... RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE`.
On SQLite it runs `DELETE FROM`.

## Debug

### `toSql`

Returns the SQL of the query with the values filled in.
The values are not quoted or escaped, so use it only to read the query.

```dart
String sql = Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').toSql();
print(sql); // SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "name" = John Wick
```

### `debug`

Prints the SQL and the values of the query when it runs.

```dart
await Actor().debug(true).where('age', 60).get();
```

To print all queries, set `debug: true` in the `ConnectionConfig`.
See [Database](index.md#config).


---

# Transactions

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/3.xdatabase/transactions/

# Transactions

A transaction runs many queries as one unit, so either all of them are saved or none of them.

`QueryBuilder.transaction()` takes a function:

- It commits when the function ends.
- It rolls back when the function throws. Then the error is thrown again.

## Use

```dart
// a transaction
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  Actor actor = Actor();
  actor.name = 'John Wick';
  await actor.save();
  await QueryBuilder.table('actor_info').insert(<String, dynamic>{
    'actor_id': actor.id,
  });
});

// return a value
int? id = await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  Actor actor = Actor();
  actor.name = 'John Wick';
  await actor.save();
  return actor.id;
});

// on another connection
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  // ...
}, connection: 'mysql');
```

- All queries and models inside the function use the transaction.
  You do not pass a transaction object around.
- A transaction inside another transaction uses a savepoint.
  See [Nested transactions](#nested-transactions).

!!! warning "MySQL"
    On MySQL and MariaDB, `CREATE`, `ALTER` and `DROP TABLE` are saved right away.
    A rollback can not undo them.

## Nested transactions

A transaction inside another transaction uses a savepoint.
It runs on the same connection as the outer one.

- When the inner function ends, its work stays in the outer transaction.
  It is saved when the outer one commits.
- When the inner function throws, only its work is undone. Then the error is thrown again.
- If you catch that error, the outer transaction goes on and can still commit.
- If you do not catch it, the outer transaction rolls back too.
- When the outer transaction rolls back, the inner work is undone too.

```dart
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await Actor().create(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Wick'});
  try {
    await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
      await Actor().create(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'Bad row'});
      throw StateError('stop');
    });
  } on StateError {
    // only 'Bad row' is undone
  }
});
// 'John Wick' is saved
```

This works on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. You can nest many levels.

- Run nested transactions one after another, not at the same time (for example in `Future.wait`).
  They share one connection.
- On MySQL and MariaDB, a `CREATE`, `ALTER` or `DROP TABLE` inside a nested transaction
  saves the outer work and ends the savepoint. Do not change the schema there.

## Connections

- Postgres and MySQL use a connection pool.
  Set the size with `maxConnectionCount` in the `extra` map of the connection.
- A transaction uses one connection of the pool. Other queries use the other connections.
- SQLite has one connection per isolate.
  While a transaction is open, the other queries of that isolate wait.
- When a model has more than one relation to load (`preload` or `eager`),
  the relation queries run at the same time outside a transaction.
  Inside a transaction, they run one after another on its connection.
- A query runs in a transaction only when you use `QueryBuilder.transaction()`.


---

# Migration

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/3.xdatabase/migration/

# Migration

A migration changes your database schema step by step, with an `up` method that makes the change and a `down` method that undoes it.

Write migrations in Dart with the [schema builder](schema.md).
The same migration then works on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite.
Plain `.sql` migrations work too.

## Create a migration

```bash
dox make:migration create_users_table
```

This makes `db/migration/2026_10_21_120000_create_users_table.dart`.
The numbers are the date and time when you run the command.

```dart title="db/migration/2026_10_21_120000_create_users_table.dart"
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

class CreateUsersTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.create('users', (Table table) {
      table.id();
      table.timestamps();
    });
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.dropIfExists('users');
  }
}
```

Add your columns in `up`, for example `table.string('email').unique();`.
See [Schema](schema.md) for all column types.

The name of the migration decides what the new file contains:

| Name | The file has |
|---|---|
| `create_users_table` | `schema.create('users', ...)` in `up`, and `dropIfExists('users')` in `down` |
| `add_avatar_to_users_table` (also `_from_`, `_in_`, `_on_`) | `schema.table('users', ...)` in `up` and `down` |
| any other name | empty `up` and `down` |

- `create:migration` does the same.
- `dox create:model Blog -m` makes the model and a `create_blogs_table` migration.

!!! info "Raw SQL and data in a Dart migration"
    `schema.driver` runs raw SQL on the same connection and transaction:
    `await schema.driver.execute("UPDATE users SET role = 'admin' WHERE id = 1");`
    Do not use models or `QueryBuilder` in a migration. They use another connection.

## The registry

An AOT build can not load a file at run time.
So Dox keeps a list of your Dart migrations in `db/migration/migrations.dart`:

```dart
// Made by `dox make:migration` and the `dox migration:*` commands.
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import '2026_10_21_120000_create_users_table.dart' as m1;

final List<MigrationEntry> migrations = <MigrationEntry>[
  MigrationEntry(
    '2026_10_21_120000_create_users_table',
    m1.CreateUsersTable(),
  ),
];
```

- `dox make:migration` and every `dox migration:*` command write this file again.
  You do not edit it.
- It lists each file named `YYYY_MM_DD_HHMMSS_name.dart` and its `class ... extends Migration`.
- The name of a migration is its file name without `.dart`. The order is by name.

The first `dox make:migration` also makes `bin/migrate.dart` in your app:

